newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FROM THE HILL-Talks deadline inches into next week.
newsitem.headline: FROM THE HILL-Talks deadline inches into next week.

text.p: It still seems to be up in the air whether New Zealand First will announce this week or next week if it will go with Labour or National. But on the scraps of evidence around a very quiet parliament late on Tuesday, the decision appears to be drifting into next week.

Reports are clearly all but finalised on the shape of deals with both sides. After Labour and NZ First caucuses in the morning (National has postponed its caucus until later in the week) the talk was of position papers/executive summaries/heads of agreement going to National and Labour later this week.

Opinions are divided on why National postponed. Perhaps the details are in place and there is nothing to talk about until they are released. Perhaps it is easier to keep them under wraps if they are not released until the last moment. Or perhaps, as one Labour MP speculated, the shape of a deal will cause such a fight and such rejection on the part of some it is better left for a single blood-letting. One NZ First MP told Reuters he expected the leaks to start later this week once the process of passing papers to Labour and National MPs got under way, while a Labour caucus source hinted an emergency caucus on Thursday may be called to discuss a draft deal.

That would leave NZ First time at the weekend and into next week to consider its response -- a process leader Winston Peters has already flagged was likely to take two days -- with the option of parliament sitting for the two days required on Tuesday and Wednesday, or Wednesday and Thursday next week.
Parliament must sit by Friday December 13 but two days are needed to elect a speaker and get the session underway with an address from the throne and the start of the address-in-reply debate.

Given that standing orders do not allow for Friday sittings (and would apparently need to be suspended earlier in the week on a sitting day allowed by standing orders -- i.e. Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday) then in effect the Friday deadline imposed by law is modified to Thursday 12th by standing orders.
Little emerged from the NZ First and Labour caucuses on Tuesday, other than indications there were still significant sticking points between Labour and NZ First over the usual issues.

These include the amount of fiscal stimulus the economy can wear, as well as some sleeping social issues such as NZ First's attraction to the housing supplement while Labour is commited to charging state house tenants market rents. Housing policy is high on the agenda for Labour leader Helen Clark.

There has always been a group in the National caucus -- seen to include young and ambitious MPs such as Roger Sowry, CHE Minister Bill English, Tony Ryall and some of the other economic "dries" -- who have reservations about doing a deal with NZ First at all.

They argue the rejuvenation of National will be easier in opposition. A rejuvenation in government with NZ First would give free-market ACT a chance to make inroads on the right and at the same time bring into power a group of MPs less committed to the compromises needed to stitch up a deal with NZ First than the current old guard led by Prime Minister Jim Bolger. Hence instability.
But a source in Labour said that there were now rumblings -- although not divisive yet -- that Labour is also beginning to question whether it really wants to do a deal with NZ First.

It is hard to believe that a long absence from the Treasury benches will not put that thought quickly to flight in Labour's case, but it is interesting that the question is being asked as a deal nears and the media begin more consistently to expect a deal with National. (Bearing in mind that any details given to the media by either side could be covert signals to the "losing" side to "give" a little more.)
It brings to mind Peters' warning before the election that in the end it may not be a question of who NZ First goes with, but who will go with NZ First.
